Wants to visit the park
Both ideas are equally valid.
Disagreements happen when we want different things.
Can you help Maya and Arjun find a solution?

actions.text: Hello everyone, and welcome to our class! Today we're starting something really important — we're going to learn how to solve problems when two people want different things. Over the next few lessons, we'll follow a short story and see if we can help two friends find a happy ending. Let's begin.
Look at the title of our page: 'The Dilemma: Movie or Park?' A dilemma is when you have to choose between two things, and both of them seem good. Let's meet the two friends in this dilemma.
This is Maya. Take a close look at her idea — Maya wants to watch a movie. Maybe she loves the big screen, the popcorn, and sitting somewhere cozy with her friends.
And this is Arjun. Arjun wants something completely different — he wants to visit the park. Maybe he's thinking about running outside, fresh air, and playing games in the sunshine.

Now here's the really important part. Both ideas are equally valid. That means Maya's wish is not silly, and Arjun's wish is not wrong. Neither one of them is being difficult — they just want different things, and that's completely normal.

This is exactly how disagreements start. A disagreement happens when we want different things. It doesn't mean someone is bad or selfish. It simply means two people have two different ideas at the same time. Have you ever felt that way with a friend or a brother or sister? I'm sure you have — it happens to everyone.

So here is our big question for today: can you help Maya and Arjun find a solution? Think quietly for a moment — what does Maya want, what does Arjun want, and could both of them matter at the same time? Hold on to your thoughts, because on the next page we're going to choose what happens next in their story.

Remember the moment we just covered — Maya wants the movie, and Arjun wants the park. Both of them feel strongly about it. So here's the big question we started to ask: could both of them matter at the same time? On this page, you get to decide what happens next.

actions.content: Watch these two feeling meters. Maya and Arjun each start at 50 — right in the middle.

actions.text: Notice the two feeling meters at the top. Maya's meter and Arjun's meter both begin at 50 out of 100. Whatever choice you make will move these numbers — and that tells us how each friend feels about what happened.

actions.content: The scene appears — read Maya and Arjun's moment first.
This is the 'What happens next?' box. Drag one choice card into it to see the outcome.
Three choices: Maya gets her way, Arjun gives in, or they listen to each other.

actions.text: You have three choices. Maya could get her way, Arjun could give in, or they could listen to each other. Before you drag anything, think for a moment — which choice would keep BOTH students feeling good? You only see the outcome after you choose, so trust your thinking. Go ahead and choose what happens next.

scenes.title: Explore the Consequences and Try Again

actions.text: We just covered the basics of different approaches to disagreements, and now we are going to explore the real-life consequences of those choices.

actions.content: Take a look at the three options available for Sam and Maya.
Showing the positive result of the Win-Win approach.
When they choose Win-Win, both friends end up feeling highly respected and satisfied.

actions.text: Notice how this outcome is the result of a structured process. Instead of just listening or giving in, we need to look for the Win-Win solution.

actions.content: The steps of the Win-Win process: listen, understand, brainstorm, check fairness, and agree freely.

actions.text: If you think there's a better way, try changing the empathy level or choosing one of the other options and see if you can lead to a similar positive result.

In the last activity, we saw what happens when one friend gets their way and the other one does not. Now let's find something better — a solution where both Maya and Arjun win. Look at the diagram on your screen.

actions.content: Start here — the shared problem both friends face.

actions.text: From the top, the diagram splits into two branches. That is exactly how the problem works: Maya has her needs, Arjun has his, and at first they look like they pull in different directions.

actions.content: One friend's needs branch out here.
Where both needs meet — the Win-Win options.

actions.text: Now follow the lines down to this middle node. This is where the two sets of needs overlap — and that overlap is where our options live. One option is to visit the park today and watch the movie another day. Another is to find a completely different activity that both friends enjoy. Notice there is more than one good answer here.

actions.content: The goal: a plan both friends freely agree to.

actions.text: And this last node is the most important part of all. A Win-Win only counts when both friends agree freely — not because one of them gave in, and not because someone was pressured. Take a moment to read the two options in the details panel, and then choose the one you think works best — or come up with your own idea that meets both needs. On the next page, you will get to apply Think Win-Win to a situation of your own.

We just covered how a Win-Win solution meets both people's needs. Now it is your turn to try it yourself. Mia and Leo are friends, but they want to play different games — Mia wants to build with blocks, and Leo wants to play a board game. Let's see whether they can find a Win-Win.

actions.content: This slider shows how clearly Mia speaks up for what she wants.
This slider shows how well Mia listens to understand what Leo wants.
One friend gets everything, the other gets nothing.
The badge names the result — this one is Win–Lose, and Leo is not happy.
Now both friends speak up, listen, and explore more ideas together.
Press Start to watch Mia and Leo act out this plan.

actions.text: Notice the difference. When one person wins and the other loses, the friendship feels shaky. When both speak up, both listen, and both explore more options, the plan feels fair. Remember the THINK WIN-WIN steps: listen to understand, respect both perspectives, explore possibilities, and choose a fair solution together. And keep this in mind — Win-Win is never about defeating someone, and it is not about always giving in. It is about finding a way where both of you can be happy. Try the sliders and presets on your own, and see how many different Win-Win plans you can create. Great work today!
